More than a third of UK organisations say technology skills gaps have cost them at least £380,000 in the past year. Among the largest firms, those turning over £73 million or more, that rises to 57%, with 15% reporting costs of £760,000 or higher.

That's from Pluralsight's annual Tech Skills Report, published this week, surveying 500 UK tech executives, IT professionals, and learning and development leaders.

The number isn't abstract. It's showing up as 40% of organisations unexpectedly outsourcing or hiring externally for project work they thought they could deliver in-house. 39% failing to deliver key projects. 30% reporting budget overruns. 27% losing a client or contract outright. Each of those is a moment where someone discovered, after the fact, that the capability they assumed existed inside the organisation didn't.

Here's the detail that doesn't fit the usual story. 85% of these organisations hired the same number of junior tech staff this year or more. This isn't a pipeline that's run dry at the recruitment stage. And yet 88% say they're worried they don't have enough junior talent coming through to close the skills gaps AI itself can't solve.

So people are coming in. The worry is about what happens to them once they're inside. 46% of technology workers say they struggle to find time for training. 28% of L&D leaders cite a lack of support from leadership as a barrier to upskilling. 53% of senior leaders admit they're unsure how to solve their own skills gaps.

Pluralsight frames this as a cycle: leaders recognise the need for new capability, employees lack the time and organisational backing to build it. That's accurate, but it understates what's actually happening underneath. An organisation can hire well, invest in tools, 94% have invested in AI tools for at least some staff, and still have no reliable picture of what its people can do a year after they walk through the door. 

The gap isn't at the hiring stage. It's in the complete absence of any ongoing, verified record of what capability actually developed, stalled, or quietly went unused.

Matthew Lloyd Davies, Pluralsight's principal security author, makes the point sharply in the context of cybersecurity specifically: skills gaps are costly because they lengthen the window before a problem is caught, and cost scales with that window staying open. 

The same logic applies more broadly. The longer an organisation goes without actually knowing what its workforce can do, the more expensive the eventual discovery becomes. £380,000 is what it costs to find out the hard way, through a failed project or a lost client. Knowing earlier isn't a training problem. It's a visibility problem.

If your organisation is investing in junior hiring and in training, what's actually tracking whether either one is closing the gap?

Your AI resume scorer told you a candidate is "strong" — but what if it produced no output, and you never knew?

When you ask an LLM to score a resume, you're relying on a contract: 200 OK + valid JSON. You assume that means "I evaluated this candidate." But the contract guarantees only that the response was well-formed.

An LLM can return HTTP 200, valid JSON, and zero output tokens — all three at once. No reasoning, no scores, no signal. Your hiring pipeline saw 200 and treated it as a real evaluation.

Why does this happen? Context limits, model confusion, prompt fatigue in batch jobs. The response looks right. The actual judgment never occurred.

The cost is silent: a strong candidate slides into the "maybe later" pile. You never know you missed them. They take a different offer.

This failure can't be caught by asking "did the model error?" It succeeded at returning a response while failing at the actual task.

When you're automating hiring, you need visibility into whether the AI step actually ran — not just whether the API call returned 200. Silent failures mean candidates scored wrong without anyone knowing. It's not a broken workflow — it's a hire you never made.

Day 1 for a senior executive is usually warm: a welcome, introductions and plenty of goodwill. Underneath it sits a performance contract with tension already built in.

The business expects early movement. The executive is hired for the experience and senior capability to work out what deserves attention first, what can wait and what may not be the issue at all.

I am a strong proponent of structured onboarding, whether the hire is senior or junior. Onboarding is broader than induction. Clear expectations, access, manager alignment and deliberate integration help people get traction faster. Ambiguity is not autonomy, and clarity does not require every intervention to be selected in advance.

A draft 30/60/90 plan I was reviewing made that tension visible. In the first 30 days, the new executive was expected to understand the customer and commercial issues, establish a baseline, review the roadmap and diagnose the constraints. The same plan also required two AI-enabled workflows to be live.

That expectation may be right. The risk appears when the whole performance contract is read together: the executive is still expected to establish where performance is constrained, yet one intervention has already been prescribed as evidence of success.

The cost can be senior time, capacity and organisational attention committed before there is enough room to establish whether that intervention addresses the right constraint, at the right point and at the right time.

This is where the bookends help. At one end is the business objective this appointment is meant to advance and why it matters now. At the other is the business outcome and value that would show the appointment is working.

What sits between them should not be vague, but neither should it be over-prescribed. The executive still has to establish where movement is being lost, what deserves priority, which intervention fits the condition and what needs to move downstream.

The more precisely we prescribe the middle, the less room remains for the senior capability we paid for.

The expectation for early movement stays. What changes is what Day 30 has to prove: can the executive connect the business objective to the constraint, the intervention chosen, the downstream movement expected and the business outcome it is meant to influence?

If the prescribed intervention survives that test, it stays. If it does not, changing course early is part of the return on hiring senior capability.

That is one practical use of the Business Constraint™ Scan around a senior appointment: testing whether the mandate, intervention and intended business result belong on the same route before the success criteria harden around one answer.

In August 2026 the Stanford Digital Economy Lab updated one of the most discussed studies on AI and employment. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen use ADP payroll records covering millions of US workers, through June 2026. Their first finding is reassuring: no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement. Their second deserves the attention of every executive committee. Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations now stands 19 percent below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers. Experienced workers in the same occupations show no comparable gap.

The mechanism matters. The adjustment comes mainly through reduced hiring of young workers rather than through layoffs, and it is concentrated in occupations where AI primarily substitutes for human tasks. Where AI primarily complements workers, employment is flat or rising. The authors are careful to call these early, descriptive indicators on US data, and they note that some patterns weaken when education is controlled for. I read it as a signal, not a verdict.

The signal is still worth acting on, because it points at an asset that rarely appears in any AI business case. Junior roles are where an organization produces its future senior expertise. Judgment about what a good contract review, a clean piece of code or a sound reconciliation looks like is built by doing the routine version thousands of times. If AI absorbs that routine work and we quietly stop hiring, we book a saving this year and draw down the pipeline that will supply the experienced people who make AI valuable in the first place.

So the question for the committee is how we rebuild the apprenticeship when the routine tasks go. That means roles where juniors work with AI on tasks that complement them, and a deliberate view of which skills we will need in five years and where they will be learned. The study suggests the complement pattern is the protective one. It is also, I suspect, the one that compounds.

Why I Don’t Let AI Agents Control Enterprise Workflows Directly

One architectural principle I keep coming back to when building AI-enabled enterprise systems is that AI can recommend what should happen next, but it should not automatically decide what is allowed to happen next. That distinction matters the moment AI stops simply answering questions and starts participating in real operational workflows.

Imagine an AI agent reviewing a case, analyzing documents, detecting an issue, and recommending an approval, escalation, payment, assignment, or status change. Technically, it is easy to let the model call an API and execute that action directly. Architecturally, I think that is the wrong boundary. Large language models are probabilistic, while enterprise workflows are usually governed by deterministic rules around current state, permissions, required evidence, approvals, deadlines, and compliance requirements.

The pattern I prefer is: Event → Context → AI Recommendation → Rules & Guards → Human Approval when required → Validated Transition → Event → Audit Trail. AI is still extremely useful in that flow. It can interpret unstructured information, summarize context, identify anomalies, prioritize work, and recommend next actions. The workflow engine, however, answers a different question: is this action actually valid?

If an AI assistant recommends moving a workflow from In Review to Approved, the system should verify that the transition is allowed, the required evidence exists, the actor has the right authority, and mandatory reviews are complete. Only then should the workflow engine execute the change. That gives the organization control, traceability, and a reliable record of what happened, who approved it, and why the system allowed it.

Recruitment is one example. In RecruitIQ, AI can assist with candidate screening, assessments, comparisons, and decision support, but I would not want an opaque model becoming the hiring authority. The system should preserve the criteria, evidence, structured evaluation, human review, decision rationale, and audit history around the final outcome. The same architectural problem appears in compliance, claims, case management, healthcare, financial operations, contract approvals, and government workflows.

This is also one of the ideas behind FlowTwin, the event-driven workflow engine I’ve been building in .NET and Azure. I want the AI layer to be powerful, but bounded, while the underlying system remains deterministic, observable, recoverable, and auditable.

The principle I keep coming back to is simple: AI recommends. The deterministic workflow engine decides what is valid. That boundary may be one of the biggest differences between an impressive AI demo and an AI system an enterprise can actually trust in production.

Strong governance is the reason some companies get real value from AI in HR while others stall.

I now treat it as a growth strategy rather than a compliance task. When you can trust your tools, explain your decisions and stand behind the outcomes, you can use AI with far more confidence than a competitor who is one bad surprise away from switching it off.

Here is what strong AI governance looks like in practice:

→ Give every AI decision a human owner. On any call that affects someone’s job or career, a named person signs off. The tool advises, and a human makes the final decision.

→ Choose tools you can explain. You should be able to say in plain words how a system reached its decision. If you can explain it, you can improve it and defend it.

→ Audit for bias on a schedule. Test a tool before you roll it out, and keep testing after. We check the finances every year and our hiring models deserve the same discipline.

→ Be transparent with your people. Tell candidates and employees where AI is used, and give them a clear route to a human. The trust you build here carries across the whole organization.

→ Hold your vendors accountable. Put testing, transparency and responsibility into the contract before go-live.

Good governance gives you the confidence to use AI fully, and to keep going when others have to pause and fix problems.

The companies that get the most from AI over the next decade will be the ones that governed it well from the start. That is why I put governance at the top of the AI priority list from day one.

On his first day, our new warehouse supervisor had no desk, no email and no Emirates ID appointment.

Nobody had done anything wrong.

He'd accepted the offer on a Thursday, due to start 10 days later. HR was waiting on the line manager to confirm the date. The line manager assumed HR had told IT. IT never got a ticket. The PRO was waiting on a signed contract that was sitting in someone's drafts folder.

Four people, each waiting on one of the others. Nobody late. Nobody careless.

This was a 48-person trading company in Mussafah, not a multinational with four layers of HR between the offer and the desk.

I counted the whole thing out afterwards. 23 steps between offer accepted and day one, spread across HR, IT, the PRO and the hiring manager. 11 of them need no human judgement at all.

That's usually the point where a client asks me about AI, and yes, those 11 come off the table fast.

But the three days this man lost weren't lost in the 11 steps. They were lost in the gaps between four people who each thought the handoff was someone else's. Automating a step nobody owns just makes the silence faster.

So the first thing I changed wasn't a tool. I gave the handoff one owner and one date, 10 working days before any start date, before anyone wrote another checklist.

In 10 years here I've never seen onboarding fail on the paperwork. It fails on the handover.

Real question for the founders and HR people reading this: how many days before a new joiner starts does your team actually confirm the IT setup and the visa appointment?

Not what the policy says. What actually happens.

Let’s stop pretending OnlineJobs.ph is revolutionary technology.
It is not.
It is a job board: searchable profiles, job posts, filters, and a recruiting workflow built with technology that has existed for decades.
Quite honestly, the first-generation Game Boy was more advanced than OnlineJobs.ph.
That is the sad part.
The original Game Boy came out in 1989. It had a processor, memory, real-time input, graphics, sound, cartridge-based software, and delivered a complete portable gaming experience on batteries.
OnlineJobs.ph is essentially a searchable directory of worker profiles and job listings. Online classifieds, job boards, forums, and early internet marketplaces established that model a long time ago.
This is not advanced AI.  
This is not modern fintech.  
This is not workforce governance.  
This is not a breakthrough anyone should feel indebted to.
Yet an entire industry has convinced Filipino professionals that access to this kind of platform is an opportunity they should be grateful for.
Clients use it because it gives them access to skilled, English-speaking Filipino professionals at rates they often could not justify at home. They call it “global hiring,” but too often the actual question is: How cheaply can I access competent people in the Philippines?
Then they act as though posting a job, sorting profiles, sending messages, and offering low rates is some kind of contribution to the country.
It is not.
The professionals on those platforms are not lucky to be discovered by an old job-board model. The platforms, recruiters, agencies, course sellers, and overseas clients are lucky that Filipinos continue to supply the intelligence, skill, loyalty, adaptability, and execution that keep businesses moving.
The technology was never the difficult part.
The real issue is that people were trained to compete inside systems they do not own, under rules they did not write, with payment structures they do not control, and with limited protection when something goes wrong.
Filipino talent does not need another ancient job board dressed up as empowerment.
It needs modern infrastructure:
•	Real worker protections.
•	Transparent pricing and accountable transactions.
•	Contracts and professional standards that protect both sides.
•	Secure, fair payment systems.
•	Technology that treats Filipino professionals as economic participants—not inventory in a searchable database.
If you are a client, stop congratulating yourself for “giving Filipinos opportunities” through a decades-old labor-marketplace model.
You are not rescuing anyone. You are accessing talent.
Pay accordingly. Treat people accordingly.

Let’s stop pretending OnlineJobs.ph is revolutionary technology.
It is not.
It is a job board: searchable profiles, job posts, filters, and a recruiting workflow built with technology that has existed for decades.
Quite honestly, the first-generation Game Boy was more advanced than OnlineJobs.ph.
That is the sad part.
The original Game Boy came out in 1989. It had a processor, memory, real-time input, graphics, sound, cartridge-based software, and delivered a complete portable gaming experience on batteries.
OnlineJobs.ph is essentially a searchable directory of worker profiles and job listings. Online classifieds, job boards, forums, and early internet marketplaces established that model a long time ago.
This is not advanced AI.  
This is not modern fintech.  
This is not workforce governance.  
This is not a breakthrough anyone should feel indebted to.
Yet an entire industry has convinced Filipino professionals that access to this kind of platform is an opportunity they should be grateful for.
Clients use it because it gives them access to skilled, English-speaking Filipino professionals at rates they often could not justify at home. They call it “global hiring,” but too often the actual question is: How cheaply can I access competent people in the Philippines?
Then they act as though posting a job, sorting profiles, sending messages, and offering low rates is some kind of contribution to the country.
It is not.
The professionals on those platforms are not lucky to be discovered by an old job-board model. The platforms, recruiters, agencies, course sellers, and overseas clients are lucky that Filipinos continue to supply the intelligence, skill, loyalty, adaptability, and execution that keep businesses moving.
The technology was never the difficult part.
The real issue is that people were trained to compete inside systems they do not own, under rules they did not write, with payment structures they do not control, and with limited protection when something goes wrong.
Filipino talent does not need another ancient job board dressed up as empowerment.
It needs modern infrastructure:
•	Real worker protections.
•	Transparent pricing and accountable transactions.
•	Contracts and professional standards that protect both sides.
•	Secure, fair payment systems.
•	Technology that treats Filipino professionals as economic participants—not inventory in a searchable database.
If you are a client, stop congratulating yourself for “giving Filipinos opportunities” through a decades-old labor-marketplace model.
You are not rescuing anyone. You are accessing talent.
Pay accordingly. Treat people accordingly. Build relationships accordingly.

Most discussions about Python in 2026 still focus on free-threading and lazy imports as the headline features. But the most practical development is something quieter and more consequential: Python is becoming a first-class language for building verifiable, safety-critical systems, and the industry is barely discussing it.

The non-obvious insight is not about speed. It is about correctness. Python 3.14s enhanced type hinting and the improved REPL are not just quality-of-life improvements. They enable a workflow where you can write a data pipeline in Polars with full type safety, annotate every function signature with precise generic constraints, and then run a static type checker that proves your pipeline cannot produce a null pointer or a type mismatch at runtime. For production AI infrastructure, this eliminates an entire category of bugs that used to surface only after deployment.

The second under-discussed development is the maturation of Python's ecosystem for reproducible, auditable software supply chains. The shift from pip to uv is not just about speed. It is about deterministic builds. Uv produces a lockfile that pins every dependency to a specific hash, and that lockfile can be cryptographically signed and verified. In 2026, teams that cannot prove exactly which version of pandas or numpy their model was trained on will fail compliance audits. The teams that embrace uv will pass those audits without additional tooling.

The most undervalued trend is Python's role in the formal verification of AI behavior. With the new type hinting capabilities, it is now possible to write runtime-verifiable contracts for model outputs. You can define a type that says "this function returns a float between 0 and 1, representing a probability," and have the type checker enforce that every call site respects that contract. This is not theoretical. It is being used in production to catch model drift and data leakage before they affect downstream systems.

For hiring managers: the candidates who can articulate why Polars lazy evaluation reduces memory pressure in a streaming pipeline, or why uvs lockfile reproducibility eliminates environment drift in ML experiments, are the ones who will build Python systems that are both fast and provably correct. They understand that in 2026, Python is not just a scripting language for quick experiments. It is a platform for building AI infrastructure that is auditable, reproducible, and safe.

I work at five monitors.

This is not a flex. It started as a solution to a problem and has since become a personality trait. (My neck would like a word.)

People assume a solo practice is a tiny version of a big firm. A guy, a desk, a filing cabinet, and a printer that jams out of spite.

Nope. I am the entire firm. Managing partner, associate, paralegal, IT department, and the guy who changes the toner. The desk reflects that.

Monitor one: the document.

Monitor two: the other side's version of the document. Same document, wearing a fake mustache.

Monitor three: whatever industry I'm learning this week, because a new client's business doesn't care that I'd never heard of it on Monday.

Monitor four: email. I've advised myself not to comment.

Monitor five: the AI, cheerfully drafting the first 80% while I argue with monitor two.

Monitor three is the one that surprises people. Thirty years in, the thing I do most is learn somebody else's business fast enough to be useful by Friday. Industrial helium one month, logistics the next, a manufacturing program in Mexico after that. You can't fake it, and you shouldn't bill for the learning. So you get quick.

Behind me: guitars. The exact number is a matter I'll be taking up with my accountant, ideally under a privilege I'm fairly sure doesn't apply.

On the desk: paper. Actual paper, in 2026. Some things I have to hold. (Also, the AI can't spill coffee on it. That's my job.)

So why should anyone thinking about hiring me care?

A firm gives you leverage. Five people touch your document and you pay for all five, including the one who is, right now, googling what your company does. The leverage is real. It's just pointed at the firm's economics, not at your deal.

I have leverage too. It's on monitor five. It doesn't bill. It doesn't need to learn your matter at your expense. And it has never once billed 0.3 for "conference re: status." (Frankly, a better colleague than some I've known.)

What's left is the part nobody has automated. Which clause fits this deal and not the last one. Which term sits quietly for three years and then detonates. When to tell a client the contract is fine but the deal isn't.

That runs on one machine, and it's the oldest one in the room. (No, not the printer.)
Now the fine print, because I don't pitch without it.

There's one of me. I don't take every matter. I refer out litigation without a moment of regret. If you need six lawyers in a room at once, you need a firm, and I'll tell you that on the first call, not the fourth.

But if you need one experienced lawyer who knows your business, answers the phone, and thinks about your deals the way your CFO thinks about your cash – that fits on this desk.

Somewhere between the paper and the guitars.

The most overlooked cost driver in supply chain for 2026 is not transportation or raw materials. It is the invisible tax of data latency between your demand signal and your procurement action.

I have spent the last year working with teams trying to operationalize ESG as a real-time constraint, not just a quarterly report. The non-obvious lesson is that Scope 3 emissions tracking is not a data collection problem. It is a supplier collaboration problem. Most teams are trying to scrape emissions data from PDFs or emails. The teams that are winning have built a shared data interface with their top suppliers, where emissions data flows directly into the procurement system alongside price and lead time. When a supplier submits a quote, the system instantly evaluates it against both cost and carbon constraints, and rejects it if it breaches the threshold.

Another trend reshaping the field is the shift toward cybersecurity as a supply chain variable, not an IT afterthought. In 2025, the most disruptive attacks were not on the ERP system itself, but on the sensor data feeding the predictive maintenance models. If your inventory optimization algorithm is relying on tampered sensor data, your "optimal" reorder point is actually a liability. The teams that are pulling ahead are embedding anomaly detection directly into the data ingestion layer, not just at the network perimeter. They treat every data point as a potential attack surface.

The human-machine collaboration piece is also more nuanced than most believe. I have seen planners successfully delegate routine exception handling to AI agents, but only when the agent is trained on the specific trade-off preferences of that planner, not a generic company policy. When the agent can explain why it chose to expedite one shipment over another using the planner's own historical reasoning, trust accelerates rapidly.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the person who can run a standard ERP module or build a single forecast model. You need someone who can design the contract-aware data pipelines that make ESG compliance operational, who understands how to model cybersecurity risk as a supply chain variable, and who can build the feedback loops that align AI agents with human decision-making. I am actively exploring the next challenge where I can apply these systems-thinking principles to build a supply chain that is resilient, not just efficient.
